segments.name: The Convent and the Merchant's Daughter

stops.name: Quito, the illegitimate daughter of the merchant Sáenz
stops.date_confidence: attested; EN and ES Wikipedia agree on 27 December 1797 and on both parents. The pin is the canonical Quito anchor inherited byte-identical from bolivar.journey.json, not a birth address: no deed or parish record consulted fixes one.
stops.campa: In the last winter of the eighteenth century a daughter is born in Quito to Simón Sáenz de Vergara, a Spanish merchant of the town, and to María Joaquina Aizpuru, who is not his wife. The city sits nine thousand feet up, wedged between the volcano Pichincha and its ravines, and it belongs entirely to Spain. The child is entered as illegitimate, which in this century is not a fact but a sentence: it will decide her schooling, her marriage, her inheritance, and the tone in which the century speaks of her afterwards. They name her Manuela.
suggested_refs: The colonial centre of Quito, San Marcos and San Sebastián quarters
Portraits of Manuela Sáenz

stops.name: Quito, the Monasterio de Santa Catalina de Siena
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Dominican convent of Santa Catalina is attested by EN and ES Wikipedia, but no source consulted gives a year of entry. The pool's earlier Conceptas stage, its 1805 date and its curriculum list appear in neither encyclopedic source and are not carried. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Dominican house of Santa Catalina takes her in and gives her what the colony gives a well-born illegitimate girl: letters, the offices of the day, and the walls. Behind those walls the wars have not started. Four years before she arrives, Alexander von Humboldt came through Quito with his barometers, weighed the volcanoes and carried off a young creole named Carlos Montúfar who would be shot in 1816 as a martyr of the independence; the convent heard none of it. Manuela learns to read in a building designed so that nothing outside can reach her.
suggested_refs: The Convento de Santa Catalina de Siena, Quito
humboldt.journey.json (Quito, January 1802)

stops.name: Quito, the officer and the leaving
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources place the departure around age seventeen, about 1814, and disagree flatly on whether she fled or was expelled. The officer is named Fausto D'Elhuyar in one account only. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: At seventeen she goes over the wall, or she is put out of it. The accounts have never agreed: one has her escaping with an officer of the garrison, the other has the nuns expelling her for the same affair. Either way the convent closes behind her and the register of respectable Quito closes with it. She is a merchant's illegitimate daughter with a scandal attached, in a city where that arithmetic is done publicly and only once. She will not be inside convent walls again until a government puts her there, in Lima, thirteen years later.
suggested_refs: The cloister and street door of Santa Catalina, Quito

stops.name: Quito, the marriage to the Englishman Thorne
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1817; ES Wikipedia gives only the year. The place is contested: some biographers put the wedding in Lima, and no encyclopedic source consulted names a city or a church. The pool's precise 27 July 1817 date at Quito's Catedral Metropolitana is uncorroborated and not carried. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Her father arranges what a scandal requires: a husband with money and no local memory. James Thorne is an English physician and merchant, roughly twice her age, and the marriage is a settlement rather than a courtship. It buys her a name, a household, and a passage to Lima where nobody has heard about the convent. She will never be free of it and will outlive him by nine years without recovering a peso of what the contract promised her. She is nineteen when she signs it, and she boards for Callao as Manuela Thorne.
suggested_refs: The Sáenz de Vergara merchant house of Quito
Marriage settlements of the late viceroyalty

segments.name: Lima, the Conspiracy and the Order of the Sun

stops.name: Callao, the arrival in the viceroyalty
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool dates the crossing to 1819 on Murray (2008), which reaches this file at second hand. Month and day defaulted. The pin is the canonical Callao anchor inherited byte-identical from san_martin.journey.json.
stops.campa: The ship comes in under the guns of the Real Felipe, the fortress that has held the throat of Spanish South America for a century. Callao is the port through which the silver of Potosí went out and the orders of Madrid came in. Manuela Thorne, twenty-one years old, walks up from the mole into the City of Kings as an English merchant's wife, which is a passport into every drawing room in the viceroyalty. Two years later San Martín's siege will bring these walls down, and she will be inside the city, not on the Spanish side of it.
suggested_refs: The Real Felipe fortress, Callao
san_martin.journey.json (Callao, the Real Felipe surrenders)
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Lima, the merchant's wife among the conspirators
stops.date_confidence: attested as to her part in the conspiracy against Viceroy José de la Serna (EN Wikipedia); no source consulted dates her entry into it. Month editorially placed after the arrival at Callao, day defaulted. The pin is the canonical Lima anchor inherited byte-identical from bolivar.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the salons of viceregal Lima the conversation runs two ways at once and she learns to hold both. Her husband's house receives royal officials; she carries what is said in it to the men plotting against Viceroy José de la Serna. The work is unglamorous and exact: names, sailing dates, the temper of a garrison, who is owed money and by whom. She is good at it for the reason that will follow her all her life, which is that nobody in the room believes a young wife from Quito is doing anything but listening.
suggested_refs: The viceregal court of José de la Serna, Lima
The Thorne residence in colonial Lima
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Lima, the Numancia regiment turned
stops.date_confidence: attested that she took part in efforts to induce colonial troops, the Numancia regiment named specifically, to defect to the patriot cause (EN Wikipedia). The pool places this in 1820 without a month or a day; both defaulted.
stops.campa: The Numancia battalion is Spain's on paper: creole rank and file under royal colors, garrisoned in Lima, waiting to be told what they are. Manuela works on them through the months of the conspiracy, and the regiment goes over whole to the patriot side. It is not a battle and it raises no monument. It is the kind of labor the independence actually consisted of, done in kitchens and corridors and doorways by people the dispatches decline to name, and it is the first time her name is attached to a military result.
suggested_refs: The Numancia battalion and its defection to the patriot army

stops.name: Lima, caballeresa del Sol
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the honor, contested as to the year: the pool's chronology said 1821 while citing a source that says 1822, and the Orden El Sol del Perú was created only by San Martín's decree of 8 October 1821. ES Wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com both date the investiture to 1822. No source gives a day; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: José de San Martín, Protector of Peru, founds an order to reward the people who made his entry into Lima possible, and he puts Manuela Sáenz into it: caballeresa del Sol, knight of the Sun. The Protector is precise about what he is doing. The men are decorated for what they did in the field and she is decorated for what she did in the city, and the decree draws no distinction between the two. It is the first time a republic on this continent gives a woman a rank for political work instead of a pension for a dead husband.
suggested_refs: The Orden El Sol del Perú, created by decree of 8 October 1821
san_martin.journey.json (the Protectorate of Peru)

segments.name: Quito, the Crown from the Balcony

stops.name: Quito, the return over the Cataguango inheritance
stops.date_confidence: attested that she returns to Quito in 1822 over the hacienda Cataguango inherited from her mother's family (Encyclopedia.com, which dates María Joaquina Aizpuru's death to April 1822). This contradicts flatly the ES Wikipedia account in which the mother died of puerperal fever shortly after the birth. Both stand in the sources; neither is resolved here. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: She comes back alone to the city that put her out, and she comes back on business. The hacienda of Cataguango stands in her mother's family, and the law now says a part of it stands in hers. The Quito she re-enters is five weeks from the end of Spanish rule and does not know it: Sucre's army is already moving up from the coast toward the volcano. She arrives as a claimant in a property suit at the age of twenty-four, and she will leave the city as something the whole continent has heard of.
suggested_refs: The hacienda Cataguango, south of Quito
Colonial inheritance suits of the Audiencia de Quito

stops.name: Pichincha, the volcano above the city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle, 24 May 1822. Her presence in Quito on the day is traditional (Rumazo González); any part in the fighting is tradition and not documented. The pool's chronology dated a combined Pichincha, Junín and Ayacucho presence to 1823, impossible for Pichincha, and pinned it at a null point in the central Peruvian montaña; that item is discarded.
stops.campa: On the flank of the volcano, in thin air above the roofs, Antonio José de Sucre breaks the royal army of Quito in a single morning. From the streets below the fighting is loud and largely invisible, a matter of smoke on the slope. Three centuries of Spain in this valley end before noon. Manuela is in the town; the patriotic biographies put her on the mountain and the documents do not. What is certain is that the road up from Guayaquil is now open, and that the man coming along it is Bolívar.
suggested_refs: The battlefield on the slopes of Pichincha above Quito
sucre.journey.json (the Pichincha campaign)
sources: Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz (1944), via the research pool

stops.name: Quito, the crown thrown from the balcony
stops.date_confidence: attested; Encyclopedia.com dates Bolívar's entry into Quito and the meeting to 16 June 1822, and bolivar.journey.json carries the same date and the pin inherited here byte-identical.
stops.campa: Bolívar enters Quito under arches, through flowers, on the sixteenth of June. From a balcony over the street a woman throws a crown of roses and laurel branches, meaning it to fall in front of his horse; it carries the whole force of the drop into his coat and strikes him in the chest. He looks up. She is still standing there with her arms out. He lifts his hat to her. She writes the throw down herself years afterwards, the aim and the miss both, and does not improve on either.
stops.quote: Cuando se acercaba al paso de nuestro balcón, tomé la corona de rosas y ramitas de laureles y la arrojé para que cayera al frente del caballo de S. E.; pero con tal suerte que fue a parar con toda la fuerza de la caída, a la casaca, justo en el pecho de S. E.
stops.quote_source: Manuela Sáenz's own account of the Quito welcome of 16 June 1822, quoted with footnote citation in the Spanish Wikipedia article 'Manuela Sáenz'; the underlying archival text was not reached
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json (Quito, the wreath from the balcony, shared pin and date)
The balconied streets of the Quito centro histórico

stops.name: Quito, the victory ball
stops.date_confidence: attested that they met and danced on the night of 16 June 1822. The venue is contested: Encyclopedia.com places the ball at the governor's palace, while the pool's geography lens named the Casa de los Larrea and conceded in the same breath that the house is traditionally identified and not documented. No house is named here.
stops.campa: That night the city gives a ball for the victory and the Liberator dances with the woman from the balcony until the candles are finished. He is thirty-eight and has been at war for twelve years; she is twenty-four and has just come back to town over a hacienda. Her husband is in Lima. What he says to her about her aim is the first sentence of theirs that anyone wrote down. They will be together eight years, and no two accounts agree on which house it started in.
stops.quote: Señora: si mis soldados tuvieran su puntería, ya habríamos ganado la guerra a España.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Simón Bolívar, addressed to Manuela Sáenz at the Quito victory ball of 16 June 1822, quoted in the Spanish Wikipedia article 'Manuela Sáenz'; the underlying document was not reached
suggested_refs: The governor's palace of Quito, 1822
The Casa de los Larrea, traditional site of the victory ball

stops.name: Quito, leaving the Englishman
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1822 (EN Wikipedia): she leaves Thorne and remains with Bolívar. No source consulted gives a month or a day. The month is an editorial placement after the June meeting, not a source date; day defaulted.
stops.campa: She does not go back down to Lima with her husband. There is no divorce to be had in this century and in this church, so the break is made without a procedure and without a document: she declines to return, and that is the whole of it. Thorne keeps the marriage on paper for another twenty-five years and she keeps nothing of it at all. What she takes instead is a place in Bolívar's household, first as the woman he will not give up and then, far more usefully to him, as the keeper of his papers.
suggested_refs: The surviving Sáenz-Thorne correspondence
Marriage and separation under colonial canon law
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Guayaquil, the quay of the two liberators
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Bolívar and San Martín interview of 26 and 27 July 1822 (bolivar.journey.json, san_martin.journey.json), whose pin is inherited here byte-identical. Manuela's own presence at Guayaquil on that date is inferred proximity only: neither file states it and no source consulted places her there. Reconstruction.
stops.campa: Five weeks after the crown, the two swords of the continent shut a door behind them on the Guayaquil waterfront and confer with no witnesses. No minute of it survives. San Martín comes out, returns to Lima, resigns the Protectorate that decorated her the year before, and leaves America for good; Bolívar keeps the war. Manuela is somewhere in the movement of people between Quito and this port in these weeks; no document places her on the quay, and none places her anywhere else either.
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json and san_martin.journey.json (the Guayaquil interview, 26-27 July 1822)
La Rotonda monument, Malecón of Guayaquil
sources: Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz (1944), via the research pool

stops.name: Lima, the keeper of the Liberator's papers
stops.date_confidence: attested: Bolívar lands at Callao and enters Lima on 1 September 1823, and bolivar.journey.json states in the same stop that Manuela follows him south. Her work as archivist of his correspondence comes through the pool's citation of Murray (2008), at second hand.
stops.campa: Bolívar comes into Lima on the first of September to be handed a war that Peru cannot finish by itself, and she comes with him. The work she takes on is not decorative. His correspondence is the nervous system of four countries at once and she orders it, copies it, files it, and knows where every sheet of it is. Officers who resent a woman in the headquarters discover that they must come to her to find out what their own commander has already ordered. She is inside the machine now, not beside it.
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json (Lima, the dictator of Peru, 1 September 1823)
The Bolivarian archive and the Cartas del Libertador
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Trujillo, the headquarters before the sierra
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool places her at the Trujillo campaign headquarters in 1824 on Murray and Rumazo González, both at second hand. No month or day is given and both are defaulted.
stops.campa: The army winters in the north while Bolívar builds it out of nothing for the third time in his life: recruits, mules, cloth, gunpowder, and a treasury made of promises. Trujillo is the last town before the sierra swallows the campaign. She is in the headquarters through the making of it, and when the columns start climbing she goes up with them, which nobody has asked of her and no regulation covers. The war is about to be settled at fourteen thousand feet by men who have not eaten properly in a year.
suggested_refs: The 1824 northern sierra campaign headquarters at Trujillo
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool
Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz (1944), via the research pool

stops.name: Pampa de Junín, the battle without a shot
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle, 6 August 1824. Her presence on the field is asserted in patriotic biography and absent from the contemporary military dispatches, a contrast the pool draws from Murray: reconstruction. This pin is not inherited; no existing journey file in the atlas carries the Pampa de Junín.
stops.campa: On the plain beside the lake, at four thousand metres, two cavalries meet and settle the matter with lances and sabres alone: in three quarters of an hour not one shot is fired. The royalists break. It is the last battle Bolívar commands in person. The patriotic biographies put Manuela on that field in uniform; the dispatches written the same week do not have her there. The two statements sit side by side in the record and are not reconciled here.
suggested_refs: The Pampa de Junín and the cavalry action of 6 August 1824
sources: Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz (1944), via the research pool
Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Lima, the colonel's commission
stops.date_confidence: attested that she is made Colonel of the Colombian army; ES Wikipedia dates it to December 1824, adopted here, and the day is defaulted. The pool's geography lens gives 1825 instead and inserts a prior honorary Sub-Lieutenancy of Hussars that neither Wikipedia mentions and which is carried only as reconstruction. The disagreement is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: The commission is signed and she is a colonel of the Colombian army: coronela, in her own name, on the establishment, at twenty-seven. It is not an honorary sash. She wears the uniform, rides with the staff, and is addressed by the rank by men who dislike being made to do it. In a war where women carry the water, cook the rations, nurse the wounded and are struck off every list afterwards, the paper exists and the paper says colonel. Within a year the only other woman on the continent holding it writes to her.
suggested_refs: The colonel's commission of Manuela Sáenz, Colombian army, December 1824

stops.name: Pampa de Quinua, the end of Spain in America
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle, 9 December 1824, on the Pampa de Quinua; the pin is inherited byte-identical from sucre.journey.json. The pool's two coordinates for this event, the city of Huamanga and a point some 68 km south of the field, are both discarded. Her presence and the field hospitals credited to her by admiring biographers are undocumented: reconstruction.
stops.campa: Below the village of Quinua, Sucre puts five thousand eight hundred men against nine thousand three hundred and destroys the royal army of the Andes in under three hours. The Viceroy of Peru is taken wounded on his own ground. Bolívar is not there; he handed the campaign to Sucre in October and waits in Lima for the courier. Three centuries of empire end on this plain. Manuela is placed here by the biographers who love her, tending the wounded, and by no document whatever.
suggested_refs: sucre.journey.json (Ayacucho, the pampa of Quinua, shared pin and date)
The equestrian monument at Quinua
sources: Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz (1944), via the research pool

stops.name: Lima, the letter from Cullco
stops.date_confidence: attested: juana_azurduy.journey.json dates the letter to 15 December 1825, written from the recovered hacienda of Cullco in Upper Peru, sourced to ideasfem.wordpress.com and EN Wikipedia. Manuela's own location on the day it was written is not documented; the pin is the canonical Lima anchor, not a recorded place of receipt.
stops.campa: From a hacienda in Upper Peru that the government has grudgingly given back to her, Juana Azurduy sits down and writes to Manuela Sáenz. Both women are colonels. Azurduy has lost a husband and four children to this war and has just been handed a rank instead of any of them. The letter thanks the republic and then says the rest plainly: that royalist officers now serve beside the men who beat them, and that the women who fought and died in the sierra will appear on no list anywhere.
suggested_refs: juana_azurduy.journey.json (Cullco, the letter to Manuela Sáenz, 15 December 1825)
The Azurduy-Sáenz correspondence of December 1825

stops.name: Palacio de la Magdalena, Lima
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool places her at Bolívar's residence at La Magdalena during 1826 on Murray, at second hand. EN Wikipedia's two stated periods, the first months of the year and again February to September, do not obviously reconcile and are not adjudicated. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: For one year they live in the same house without pretending otherwise. Bolívar governs Peru from the country palace at La Magdalena, and she is in it, sorting the correspondence of a man who is at that moment dictator of Peru, president of Colombia, and author of a constitution for a country named after him. Lima society is scandalized in the particular way that requires attending anyway. It is the longest stretch of ordinary life the two of them ever have, and it runs out in September.
suggested_refs: The Palacio de la Magdalena, Pueblo Libre, Lima
The Bolivian constitution of 1826
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Lima, the mutiny of the Third Division
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool dates the Third Division mutiny to 25 January 1827. Murray has her confronting the mutineers in Bolívar's absence, while EN Wikipedia instead has her imprisoned in a convent for political activity on his behalf. Both accounts are carried as reconstruction and are not reconciled.
stops.campa: The Colombian troops garrisoned in Lima turn on their own government in the night, and Peru discovers that it no longer wants the Liberator at any price. Bolívar is a thousand miles north. One account has Manuela walking into the barracks to face the mutineers herself; another has her arrested that same week for what she has been doing on his behalf in the city. The Lima she conspired for six years ago is now conspiring against her, in the same drawing rooms and with several of the same people.
suggested_refs: The mutiny of the Colombian Third Division, Lima, January 1827
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Lima, the convent as a prison
stops.date_confidence: attested that she is held by the Peruvian authorities in February 1827 and imprisoned in a Lima convent; which convent is not agreed in the sources consulted, and no day is given. Day defaulted. Release in March and expulsion from Peru in April are attested by EN Wikipedia.
stops.campa: She is taken by the Peruvian government and put behind convent walls for the second time in her life, at twenty-nine, for the opposite offense. The first time it was an affair; this time it is a politics. Which house holds her the sources do not agree on, and the atlas does not invent one. In March they let her out. In April they expel her from Peru altogether, and the country whose independence San Martín decorated her for closes its ports against her.
suggested_refs: The convents of colonial Lima used as political prisons
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool
Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz (1944), via the research pool

stops.name: Guayaquil, the road north
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool records Guayaquil as a customary waypoint on the route between Lima and Bogotá rather than as a documented stage of her journey. No source consulted dates her passage. The month is an editorial placement after the April expulsion; day defaulted.
stops.campa: Expelled, with the Order of the Sun still in her name and no country obliged to take her, she goes north the only way there is: coastal ships to Guayaquil, then the road up through the cordillera. This is the port where the two liberators shut a door on each other five years ago, and the port her own Ecuador will use eight years from now to refuse her entry. She passes through it twice more in her life, and both times she is going somewhere that does not want her.
suggested_refs: The Pacific coastal route between Callao and Guayaquil
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Quito, passing through her own city
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool records a stage in Quito on the overland road north, noted by biographers without detail. No source consulted dates it. The month is an editorial placement between the Guayaquil passage and the arrival at Bogotá; day defaulted.
stops.campa: The road to Bogotá runs through Quito, and so she is home for the last time. The convent that put her out is standing. The hacienda she came back to claim in 1822 is standing. Her father is in the city. Nothing in the sources says whom she saw or how long she stayed, and the biographers who record the stage record nothing else about it. She goes on north over the Colombian cordillera, and she does not see Ecuador again for eight years, and then only from a ship.
suggested_refs: The overland royal road from Quito to Santafé de Bogotá
sources: Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz (1944), via the research pool

stops.name: Bogotá, arrival in the capital of Gran Colombia
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool places her arrival in Bogotá in 1827 on Murray, at second hand, with no month or day. Month is an editorial placement at the end of the journey north; day defaulted. The pin is the canonical Bogotá anchor inherited byte-identical from bolivar.journey.json.
stops.campa: She comes into a cold city at eight thousand feet where the union is already coming apart. Bolívar holds it together by presence and by decrees that grow more absolute as his authority thins; against him stand the vice president, Francisco de Paula Santander, and the lawyers. She takes a house near the Palacio de San Carlos, in the quarter where the Spanish shot Policarpa Salavarrieta ten years ago for carrying messages, and does what she has always done: keeps the papers, hears everything, and makes exact enemies.
suggested_refs: policarpa_salavarrieta.journey.json (the 1817 execution, same few streets)
The colonial centre of Bogotá around the Palacio de San Carlos
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Bogotá, Santander shot in effigy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the party of 10 August 1828 at which Sáenz staged a mock execution of Santander in effigy is the probable original of the pool's separate 'August 1828 masked-ball plot against Bolívar', an episode the ES Wikipedia article on the Conspiración Septembrina does not contain. Carried here as the effigy scandal and not as a foiled assassination attempt.
stops.campa: At a party in August she has an effigy of Francisco de Paula Santander set up and shot. It is a joke, and it is also a public execution of the second man in the republic, carried out by a woman who holds no office at all. Bogotá forgives neither half of that. Six weeks later, when men come through the palace with knives, every person in the city knows exactly who she is and exactly what she thinks of the vice president's party. In six years his government will expel her, and the charge will be conspiracy.
suggested_refs: The Bogotá party of 10 August 1828 and the Santander effigy

stops.name: Palacio de San Carlos, the window
stops.date_confidence: attested; EN and ES Wikipedia, Murray and Rumazo González agree on the night of 25 September 1828, and bolivar.journey.json carries the same date and the pin inherited here byte-identical. The pool's generic Bogotá coordinate, some 12 km north of the palace, is discarded. The sources have Bolívar jumping on her urging; the pool's wording, that she pushed him out, overstates them.
stops.campa: Past midnight the conspirators kill the sentries and come up the stairs. She wakes him, gets him dressed and armed, and argues him out of the thing he wants to do, which is to open the door with a sword in his hand and die properly. He goes out the window into the street below. She opens the door herself and stands in it, and they beat her and go past her into an empty room. Under a bridge over the San Agustín the Liberator of half a world stands three hours in the water, listening to the city hunt him.
stops.quote: DETENTE, ESPECTADOR, UN MOMENTO / Y MIRA EL LUGAR POR DONDE SE SALVÓ / EL PADRE Y / LIBERTADOR DE LA PATRIA / SIMÓN BOLÍVAR / EN LA NEFANDA NOCHE SEPTEMBRINA / 1828
stops.quote_source: Commemorative inscription at the Palacio de San Carlos, Bogotá, marking the window; Spanish text per the Fundación Empresas Polar Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela, 'Atentado del 25 de septiembre de 1828', which also gives the Latin original
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json (Bogotá, the night of September, shared pin and date)
The window and plaque of the Palacio de San Carlos

stops.name: Bogotá, the name he gives her
stops.date_confidence: the date is the morning after the attempt. Reconstruction on the wording: the epithet 'Libertadora del Libertador' is ubiquitous in popular and scholarly accounts and could not be verified in this session as a direct quotation from any primary or archival source. bolivar.journey.json carries it in the form used here, sourced to O'Leary's Memorias and to Sáenz's own accounts.
stops.campa: They find him at dawn, soaked through and alive, and he is told what she did at the door. The name he gives her is not a compliment and not a pet name: Libertadora del Libertador, the woman who liberated the Liberator. It is a title of exactly the same grammatical order as his own, and there is no other like it on the continent. It also settles publicly, in front of the government and the army, the question his enemies had meant to settle that night with knives.
stops.quote: You are the Liberatrix of the Liberator.
stops.quote_source: Simón Bolívar to Manuela Sáenz after the night of 25 September 1828, as carried in bolivar.journey.json from O'Leary, Memorias, and from Sáenz's own accounts
suggested_refs: O'Leary, Memorias, on the night of 25 September 1828
bolivar.journey.json (the naming)

stops.name: Bogotá, the resignation and the road out
stops.date_confidence: attested for 8 May 1830, the definitive resignation and Bolívar's departure from Bogotá, carried independently in bolivar.journey.json. The pool dated the final resignation to January 1830, which is in fact the date of the 20 January address to the Congreso Admirable at which he offered to step down; the congress accepted in late April. Both dates recorded.
stops.campa: Venezuela secedes and proscribes him by name. The congress takes his resignation, and on the eighth of May he rides out of Bogotá toward the river and the sea with a small escort and a chest of thinning silver, the crowds silent, his enemies writing on the walls. She stays in the capital. They have been together eight years. He has seven months left, and the letters crossing between the Magdalena and Bogotá in that time are the last of the correspondence she spent a decade keeping in order.
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json (Bogotá, resignation and the road out, 8 May 1830)
The Congreso Admirable, January to May 1830

stops.name: Bogotá, the letter to the newspaper
stops.date_confidence: attested for 23 June 1830 (Encyclopedia.com). The text of the letter was not reachable in this research pool and is therefore not quoted here: a stated gap.
stops.campa: With Bolívar gone down the river and the capital's press free at last to print whatever it likes about the pair of them, she writes to a Bogotá paper and signs her name to it. She does not apologize for the household, the uniform, the effigy or the door. The letter is an act of the same species as standing in that doorway: it makes her visible and it asks for nothing. The government will need four more years to be finished with her, and it spends the first of them being publicly answered.
suggested_refs: The Bogotá press of 1830 and the Sáenz letter of 23 June

stops.name: Santa Marta, the death of the Liberator
stops.date_confidence: attested: 17 December 1830 at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino, of tuberculosis (EN Wikipedia); bolivar.journey.json carries the same date and the pin inherited here byte-identical. The pool asserted a source conflict between 10 and 17 December; that conflict is spurious and is not carried, 10 December being the day he dictated his will and issued his last proclamation. The quotation is undated in its source and is placed here.
stops.campa: On a sugar estate outside Santa Marta, in a borrowed bed, in a house lent to him by a Spanish royalist, Bolívar dies at forty-seven of the lungs. The republic he made has already dissolved. The last thing he wrote said that he had ploughed the sea. Manuela is eight hundred miles inland at Bogotá when the news comes up the road, and she has twenty-six years left in which to defend a dead man to people who would greatly prefer that he stayed dead and quiet.
stops.quote: Vivo adoré a Bolívar, muerto lo venero.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Manuela Sáenz on her devotion to Bolívar after his death, quoted in the Spanish Wikipedia article 'Manuela Sáenz', section 'Exilio y muerte'; the underlying primary document was not located
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json (Santa Marta, death of the Liberator, shared pin and date)
The Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino

stops.name: Bogotá, expelled by decree
stops.date_confidence: attested that she is expelled from New Granada as a hostile political figure under the government of Francisco de Paula Santander; Encyclopedia.com dates the expulsion to 1834 while EN Wikipedia's chronology implies 1835. Flagged, not resolved. Month and day defaulted. Note that the government which moved against her immediately after Bolívar's death was Urdaneta's: Santander was in European exile until October 1832.
stops.campa: Santander is president now, home from Europe, and the man she had shot in effigy signs the order. She is expelled from Colombia on a charge of conspiring against the state, which in her case means having been the household of the wrong dead man and having said so in print over her own name. She leaves by the Magdalena, the same river Bolívar went down to die on. She is thirty-six, a colonel of an army that no longer exists, of a country that no longer exists.
suggested_refs: The expulsion decree against Manuela Sáenz, New Granada
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the ship out
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pool records the Cartagena passage as her route out of Colombian territory without a date. Month is an editorial placement after the expulsion decree; day defaulted. The pin is the canonical Cartagena anchor inherited byte-identical from bolivar.journey.json.
stops.campa: She leaves the continent from the walls where Bolívar, already dying, was handed the news that Sucre had been shot from ambush in the Berruecos and cried out that the blood of Abel was spilled. Four years on, the interests that arranged that killing hold the government now expelling her. She goes aboard for Jamaica with what she can carry. The archive she kept in order for a decade is scattered by now between three governments and her own trunks, and it is the trunks that will burn.
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json (Cartagena, the blood of Abel, shared pin)
The walls and port of Cartagena de Indias
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Kingston, the exiles' town
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Jamaican exile (Murray, via the pool, at second hand), dated 1834 to 1835 with no month. Month is an editorial placement after the Cartagena passage; day defaulted. The pin is the canonical Kingston anchor inherited byte-identical from bolivar.journey.json.
stops.campa: Kingston keeps a standing population of Spanish American exiles, men on the losing side of whichever revolution went wrong most recently, waiting on a change of government that will let them home. Nineteen years earlier Bolívar sat in this same town, penniless and twice beaten, and wrote out the letter that mapped the future of the hemisphere. She sits in it on the far side of that future. What she is waiting for is not a change of government but a single piece of paper, a passport into Ecuador, and the man who will refuse it is already president there.
suggested_refs: bolivar.journey.json (Kingston, the Jamaica Letter, shared pin)
The Spanish American exile community of Kingston
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Guayaquil, the passport revoked
stops.date_confidence: attested that President Vicente Rocafuerte revoked her passport and barred her entry to Ecuador in 1835 (EN Wikipedia; Murray via the pool). No month or day is given in the sources consulted and both are defaulted. The quotation is dated 1835 by its source and is not tied to a specific document about her.
stops.campa: She comes back to the port she has passed through three times already and asks to go home to Quito. The president of Ecuador, Vicente Rocafuerte, refuses. He cancels her passport, and he explains himself in a sentence that states plainly what the new republics have by now decided about the women who made them. She is turned around on the water, within sight of the country she was born in. She is thirty-seven years old, she holds the Order of the Sun and a colonel's commission, and she never sets foot in Ecuador again.
stops.quote: It is the women who most promote the spirit of anarchy in these countries.
stops.quote_source: Vicente Rocafuerte, president of Ecuador, 1835, cited to Sarah C. Chambers, 'Republican Friendship: Manuela Sáenz Writes Women into the Nation, 1835-1856', Hispanic American Historical Review 81:2 (2001), per the English Wikipedia article 'Manuela Sáenz'; the Chambers article itself was not reachable
suggested_refs: The Rocafuerte administration and the political exiles of 1835
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Paita, the port at the edge
stops.date_confidence: attested that she settles at Paita in 1835 and remains there for the rest of her life (EN Wikipedia; Murray via the pool). No month or day is given; the month is an editorial placement after the Guayaquil refusal, day defaulted. The epithet quoted is traditional, not a documented utterance of Bolívar's.
stops.campa: Paita is a whaling port on a desert coast: three hundred houses of cane and mud between the cliff and the water, no river, no rain, drinking water carried in from seven miles off. Barred from Ecuador and from Colombia, she stops here because it is the first town on the Peruvian side of the line. She sells tobacco and candied fruit, embroiders, and writes and translates letters for the English and American whalers who put in for water. She is thirty-seven, and she will be here twenty-one years.
stops.quote_source: Traditional epithet attached to Manuela Sáenz, 'the lovable madwoman', in wide published circulation (Chirinos, 'Manuela, la «amable loca»'; García Brandt, 'La Coronela, la amable loca del Libertador'; EN Wikipedia citing Mathew Lyons, History Today 70:7, 2020). Its frequent attribution to Bolívar could not be verified in any reachable source
suggested_refs: The port of Paita on the Peruvian desert coast
Whaling logs of the Pacific fleet touching at Paita
sources: Pamela Murray, For Glory and Bolívar (2008), via the research pool

stops.name: Pativilca, the murder of James Thorne
stops.date_confidence: attested that Thorne was murdered at his hacienda in Pativilca in 1847; no month or day is given in the sources consulted and both are defaulted. Correction carried: the 8,000 pesos she could not recover was her dowry, not a share of his estate, per ES Wikipedia. The pin is the canonical Pativilca anchor inherited byte-identical from bolivar.journey.json.
stops.campa: The husband she left twenty-five years ago is murdered on his estate down the coast. The marriage was never dissolved, so she is his widow in law and entitled in law to the eight thousand pesos of dowry she brought into it. She recovers none of it. Pativilca is the town where Bolívar, skeletal with fever in 1824, was asked by a visitor what on earth he meant to do now, and answered: triumph. Both men are dead, and she is in a cane house in Paita selling tobacco.

stops.name: Paita, Garibaldi at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested that Garibaldi visited her at Paita, dated 1851 by the Spanish Wikipedia article 'Paita' and consistent with his arrival at Lima late in 1851 and his departure for Canton on 10 January 1852. The pool's two dates, 1850 and April 1846, are both impossible: in 1846 he was fighting in the Uruguayan Civil War. Month and day defaulted. The pool's claim that their conversations shaped his republican convictions is unsourced and is not carried.
stops.campa: A sea captain in his forties comes up from the port and asks for the lady who was with Bolívar. Giuseppe Garibaldi buried Anita on the road out of Rome two years ago, has a price on his head in three countries, and is working his passage across the Pacific toward Canton. Manuela is fifty-three and receives him in a chair she can no longer get out of unaided. He sits in a cane house on a desert coast with the woman who held the door at San Carlos, and neither of them is on the way home.
suggested_refs: anita_garibaldi.journey.json (the death on the road from Rome, 1849)
Garibaldi's Pacific voyage of 1851-1852

stops.name: Paita, the diphtheria
stops.date_confidence: attested for 23 November 1856; EN Wikipedia gives her age as 58 and ES Wikipedia as nearly 59, and both agree on the date.
stops.campa: Diphtheria comes into the port and goes through it the way epidemics go through towns with one doctor and water hauled in by mule. She dies of it on the twenty-third of November, fifty-eight years old, in the house she has kept for twenty-one years on the money from tobacco and letters. Nobody in Lima or Bogotá or Quito is told for weeks. The Order of the Sun and the colonel's commission are in the house with her, and so is the correspondence of the Liberator, and both the decorations and the letters have one night left.
suggested_refs: The Paita diphtheria epidemic of 1856

stops.name: Paita, the common grave and the fire
stops.date_confidence: attested that her body was buried in a communal mass grave and her belongings burned as a sanitary measure (EN Wikipedia). Correction carried: the pool stated that her body was burned, conflating the two. The date is the day after her death; no source consulted gives a burial date. The extent of the documentary loss is reconstruction, since substantial Sáenz-Bolívar correspondence survives and was published.
stops.campa: The sanitary rule in an epidemic is the same everywhere on this coast: the body into the common pit with the others, the effects into a fire in the yard. They burn the trunks. An unknown quantity of the correspondence of the man who made five republics goes up in a Paita courtyard, together with the uniform, the decoration, and every paper that could have told anyone which grave in the pit was hers. Nothing of her body is ever recovered or identified again.
suggested_refs: The common burial ground of Paita
Vicente Lecuna, Papeles de Manuela Sáenz (1945), from the surviving correspondence

stops.name: Quito, the museum on Calle Junín
stops.date_confidence: attested that Carlos Álvarez Saá founded the Museo Manuela Sáenz in Quito's centro histórico in 1992 (ES Wikipedia); no month or day is given and both are defaulted. Reconstruction on two counts: his Manuela: sus diarios perdidos y otros papeles appeared in 1995 and the authenticity of those diaries is contested by historians, and no consulted source presents the Calle Junín building as her birth house.
stops.campa: A collector opens a house on Calle Junín, in the quarter of San Marcos, and fills it with what he has gathered of her: papers, portraits, a room reconstructed. The city that expelled her from a convent, that she came back to as a claimant in a property suit, that refused her a passport home, now shows visitors a building and calls it hers. Whether she was born in it, no deed says. Whether the diaries published three years later are hers, the historians do not agree. The house stands regardless.
suggested_refs: The Museo Manuela Sáenz, Calle Junín, Quito
Carlos Álvarez Saá, Manuela: sus diarios perdidos y otros papeles (1995)

stops.name: Panteón Nacional, Caracas: the soil from Paita
stops.date_confidence: attested for the state ceremony of 5 July 2010, at which symbolic remains consisting of soil taken from her presumed burial site at Paita were interred at the Panteón Nacional near Bolívar. The pin is the canonical Panteón anchor inherited byte-identical from miranda.journey.json; the pool's generic Caracas coordinate, some 3.5 km off, is discarded.
stops.campa: A coffin of Paita earth travels overland through Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Venezuela behind an honor guard, and on the fifth of July a state ceremony lays it in the Panteón Nacional a few metres from Bolívar. There is nothing in the box but soil, because there is nothing else to put there. In the same building Francisco de Miranda has a sarcophagus carved with its doors standing open and empty, because Cádiz never gave back his bones either. Two of the great graves of this pantheon hold no one.
suggested_refs: miranda.journey.json (Caracas, Panteón Nacional: the open cenotaph, shared pin)

stops.name: Caracas, the Rosa Roja de Paita
stops.date_confidence: attested that a fourteen-metre sculpture titled 'Rosa Roja de Paita' was unveiled beside Bolívar's mausoleum in Caracas in 2013 (ES Wikipedia); no month or day is given and both are defaulted. The Ecuadorian posthumous generalship is dated 25 May 2007 by EN Wikipedia and 22 May 2007 by ES Wikipedia, a contradiction not resolved here.
stops.campa: Fourteen metres of red steel go up beside the mausoleum: a rose, for the port where she sold tobacco for twenty-one years and was tipped into a common pit. Ecuador has made her a general by now, posthumously, on the anniversary of Pichincha; Venezuela has made her a division general. She held one rank in her lifetime, coronela, signed in Peru in December 1824, and she spent the last twenty-one years of that life unable to enter any of the countries whose armies now promote her.
